_readme: The Garbage Plate, for /garbage-plate.html. The channel is named after this
dish and there was no page about it.
WHY THIS FILE IS MOSTLY SOURCES. Tim asked for this page because the
existing coverage of the dish is thin: listicles, and a paragraph of
half-remembered origin story repeated from site to site. The way to beat
that is not to write it better, it is to write it CHECKABLE, which is the
same thing /first-partner-illustration-collection.html and every price page
on this site do. So every historical claim below carries the source it came
from and the date that source was read, and the page prints all of it.
NOTHING GOES IN HERE FROM MEMORY. The dish has a real documented origin, a
real family business behind it and a real federal trademark, so there is no
excuse for a recalled fact. If a claim cannot be sourced it is left out, and
several were: see `notSourced` below, which exists so nobody re-researches
them and so the page can say plainly what it does not know.
THE PRIMARY SOURCES ARE THE GOOD ONES AND THEY ARE NAMED FIRST. The United
States Patent and Trademark Office publishes the whole trademark file, which
settles the date question the food writing keeps getting slightly wrong, and
Nick Tahou Hots' own fax order form is the business itself listing every
component of its own plate. Those two carry most of the page's weight.
ROCHESTER NY ONLY, and its ring, exactly as data/shops.json says: ours are
146xx. Rochester MINNESOTA and Rochester MICHIGAN both exist and both
outrank us in a national search. Check the zip on every entry.
HOURS ARE NOT PUBLISHED UNLESS THEY ARE CONFIRMED, same rule as shops.json,
and the cost of being wrong is the same: somebody drives across town to a
locked door. A confirmed hour is one the BUSINESS states about ITSELF on its
own site or its own ordering page. Yelp, Google, TripAdvisor and the
directories are not evidence and are not used here even once. Where the
hours are not confirmed the entry carries `hoursUnknown` and the page says
so in as many words rather than leaving a quiet blank.
THE LIST IS A LIST AND NOT A RANKING, and `listNote` says how it was chosen.
Ordering somebody else's restaurants by quality is not a claim this site can
source, and it is not one Tim asked for either. Nick Tahou Hots is first
because it is the originator and holds the trademark, which is a fact rather
than a verdict; everything after it is alphabetical.
THERE ARE PHOTOGRAPHS NOW, AND THE PARAGRAPH THAT USED TO SIT HERE IS WORTH
reading before you write another one like it. It said: "This site has no
license for a photograph of a building or of a plate of food. A picture of a
restaurant is somebody's copyright, and Street View imagery is licensed in a
way a static site with no keys in it cannot meet." Every sentence of that is
still true. The CONCLUSION was not, and the failure is the one this file
warns about everywhere else: a true statement about the candidates somebody
had looked at got written as a statement about the subject. Restaurant sites,
food blogs and Street View had been looked at. Wikimedia Commons had not, and
it holds eleven photographs of this dish and of the restaurant it comes from,
ten of them CC BY, CC BY-SA or public domain.
SO `photos` BELOW HOLDS TEN, added 20 August 2026, and every one was verified
by loading that file's OWN description page on Commons rather than trusting a
search result that claimed a license. The photographer, the license, the
license url, the file page and the date it was read sit beside every one, in
the same shape as `sources`, and scripts/sync-plate-photos.py re-reads all of
it from Commons on every run and refuses to write anything whose license,
author or license url has moved since. `photosRejected` says what was checked
and left out, and why, exactly as `checkedAndLeftOut` does for restaurants.
CREDIT IS A CONDITION OF THE LICENCE AND IT IS PRINTED UNDER THE PICTURE.
CC BY and CC BY-SA both require the photographer's name, the license and a
LINK to that license. A photo record naming an attribution license with no
`licenseUrl` fails the build rather than rendering, because a credit we
cannot complete is a license we cannot meet.
NOTHING IS CROPPED. Resizing and re-encoding for delivery is not an adapted
work under any of these licenses; cropping is, and four of the ten are
ShareAlike. Where the layout wants a 4:3 shape it gets it with object-fit,
which changes what is displayed and not what is distributed.
TIM'S OWN PHOTOGRAPHS ARE STILL THE BEST ANSWER for the eight restaurants
that have none. He photographs things for a living and lives here, and a
picture of Chili Hots or Fairport Hots does not exist under a free license
anywhere. The schema and the card layout take one the day it exists: add it
to `photos` with `where` set to "place:<the name on the card>".
TWO DATES AND THEY ARE NOT INTERCHANGEABLE. `published` is the day this
page first went out, 20 August 2026, and it does not move again; `updated`
is the day the research was last re-read and it moves whenever anything in
here does. The Article node in scripts/build-garbage-plate.mjs spends the
first as datePublished and the second as dateModified, which is the pair
every other Article on the site carries. Do not point both at `updated`: a
page that claims it was written today every time somebody corrects a phone
number is telling a search engine it has no history.

sources.name: United States Patent and Trademark Office, TSDR record for serial 74189085
sources.note: The federal trademark file for GARBAGE PLATE. This is the government's own record and it is the only source on the page that cannot be a retelling of another source.

sources.name: Nick Tahou Hots, garbageplate.com
sources.note: The restaurant's own site. Small, and it quotes Wikipedia for its own history, which is worth knowing before treating it as the last word on the founder.

sources.name: Nick Tahou Hots, printable fax order form
sources.note: The business listing every component of its own Garbage Plate, in its own words, as boxes you tick. It is the best single source on the page for what is actually on one.

sources.name: Rochester & Genesee Valley Railroad Museum, "Nick Tahou and the BR&P Connection", Otto M. Vondrak, 4 March 2021
sources.note: A railroad museum on the building, which is the half of the story the food writing skips.

sources.name: Tasting Table, "The Rochester Garbage Plate Is A Delicious Hot Mess", Robyn Song, 9 March 2024
sources.note: On the record with Alex Tahou, the founder's grandson. Every quote attributed to the family on this page comes from here.

sources.name: 13WHAM, "Rochester Red Wings to become the Rochester Plates to honor the Garbage Plate", 4 July 2017
sources.note: Local television on the ANNOUNCEMENT: it is dated 4 July 2017, five weeks before the game, so it is the source for the plan and for Dan Mason's words and not for the game having happened.

sources.name: Spectrum News NY1, "Red Wings serve up history as Rochester Plates", 10 August 2017
sources.note: Filed at 11:26pm on the night of the game itself, which is what makes it the source for the game having actually been played rather than only announced.

sources.name: Visit Rochester, "What is That? A Guide to The Rochester Garbage Plate"
sources.note: Monroe County's own tourism board. Useful for what a plate is generally understood to be around here, and for which restaurants it names.

sources.name: dogTown Hots, its own menu
sources.note: The Monroe Avenue shop listing its own plates, under two headings that both say Junkyard: Junkyard Plates and Junkyard Dog Plates. It is the only business on this page that files the dish under that word.

sources.name: Steve T. Hots & Potatoes, stevethots.com
sources.note: The other Tahou counter, on Lyell Avenue, and the second business on this page to publish its own plate build. Its menu states the rule in one line: two sides, and the hot sauce, mustard and onions come as standard.

sources.name: Bill Gray's, gluten free menu (PDF on their own site)
sources.note: A third independent statement of the same build, from a chain with thirteen locations: GREAT PLATES, described as a cheeseburger or hot dog served over 2 side orders.

history.head: A hot dog stand on West Main Street
history.body: Nick Tahou Hots dates itself to 1918, and it is the restaurant itself saying so: the front page of its own site carries the line "A Rochester tradition since 1918!" and not much else. The shop was called West Main Texas Hots before it was called anything else.

history.head: The one fact the sources disagree about
history.body: Nick Tahou Hots' own site quotes Wikipedia saying the restaurant "was founded by its namesake, Nick Tahou, who died in 1997 after running the establishment for over 50 years". Wikipedia's article today says something different: that Alexander Tahou, a Greek immigrant, founded it in 1918 and named it for his son Nick. Both cannot be right, and a business quoting an encyclopedia about its own founder is not the same as a business stating it. This page prints the disagreement rather than picking a winner.

history.head: It was hots and potatoes, and the beans were cold
history.body: The dish did not start as a Garbage Plate and did not start with most of what is on one now. Alex Tahou, the founder's grandson, described the original to Tasting Table in 2024.
history.quote: The original plate was hot dogs called hots and potatoes. It was hot dogs, home fries, cold beans, not hot, and two pieces of Italian bread and butter

history.head: The restaurant moved into a railroad station
history.body: The building at 320 West Main Street was never built to be a restaurant. The Rochester & Genesee Valley Railroad Museum records that its oldest part went up in 1877 as offices for the Pitkin Building and Monumental Steam Stone Works, that the railroad bought it in 1881 and expanded it into a passenger terminal, and that the Buffalo, Rochester & Pittsburgh became part of the Baltimore & Ohio system in 1932. Tahou bought the station in September 1963 for $43,000, and the move down the block waited until the original shop was demolished in 1968.

history.head: College kids named it, and the family fought it
history.body: Nobody at the restaurant chose the word. Students coming out of the bars would point at somebody else's dinner and order it by description, and the description stuck hard enough that the family gave up and put it on the sign.
history.quote: Guys would come in after drinking, and they'd see somebody that had a plate, have no idea what it was, and just say, give me a plate with all that garbage on it

history.head: GARBAGE PLATE became a federal trademark
history.body: This is the part of the story that is written down in a government file rather than retold, and the dates in that file are worth having exactly right. Nick Tahou Hots, Inc. of 320 West Main Street filed for the mark GARBAGE PLATE on 29 July 1991. It registered on 18 August 1992 as registration number 1,708,448 on the Principal Register, in class 029, and it is still live: the record shows the registration has been renewed.
history.quote: prepared entrees consisting primarily of one of the following, hot dogs without buns, hamburgers without buns, steak, pork chops, sausage, ham, fish or eggs and processed potatoes and processed beans
history.quoteWho: the registration's own description of the goods

history.head: Which is why everybody else sells a trash plate
history.body: One restaurant owns the name, so every other kitchen in Rochester serving the same idea calls it something else. Trash plate, Rochester plate, sloppy plate, junkyard plate at dogTown, and at the vegan place, a compost plate. The dish is nobody's property and the two words are, which is the whole reason the menus around here read like a thesaurus. Alex Tahou put the position plainly in 2024.
history.quote: We're trademarked, and we're still the only garbage plate

history.head: The baseball team renamed itself after it
history.body: For one home game on 10 August 2017 the Rochester Red Wings played as the Rochester Plates, in caps and jerseys with a Garbage Plate on them. 13WHAM carried the announcement five weeks out and Spectrum News NY1 filed from the ballpark on the night, which is how this page knows the game was played and not just planned. Their general manager Dan Mason told 13WHAM why, and it is as good a one line summary of the dish's standing in this city as anybody has managed.
history.quote: There is nothing more Rochester than the Garbage Plate. There isn't another food item that Rochesterians are more proud of or that is more celebrated in our city than the Garbage Plate and we can't wait to take the field as the Plates!
history.quoteWho: Dan Mason, Red Wings general manager

notSourced: WHEN THE FIRST GARBAGE PLATE WAS SERVED. Not the restaurant, the dish. Nothing reachable states a date for it, the accounts that give one give a decade, and the trademark file records when the NAME was filed rather than when the food was first sold. So this page dates the restaurant and the trademark and says openly that the dish's own start date is not documented.

THAT THE PLATE IS 100 YEARS OLD. 13WHAM's 2017 story says the Garbage Plate marked its 100th anniversary that year, which would put it at 1917, while the restaurant dates ITSELF to 1918 and the dish was called something else for most of a century. An anniversary of the shop is not an anniversary of the dish and this page does not merge them.

THE HOT SAUCE RECIPE, AND WHERE IT CAME FROM. Several retellings say the meat sauce came from a Mexican friend's family recipe. Every version of that traces back to the same handful of articles rather than to the family, none of the sources reachable here states it first hand, and a recipe's origin is exactly the kind of claim that hardens by repetition. Left out.

CALORIE COUNTS. Numbers between 1,000 and 3,000 are quoted all over the internet for a plate. No restaurant publishes one, the plate is built to order out of four possible sides and ten possible meats, so there is no single dish to count, and this site does not print a number it cannot source.

EATER'S 2017 FEATURE AND THE DEMOCRAT AND CHRONICLE'S 2020 PIECE. Both are cited by Wikipedia as the source for several of the claims above and neither could be fetched on 20 August 2026, so nothing on this page rests on either. If a later editor can read them, the founder question in the history above is the thing to settle.

anatomy.intro: There is no fixed recipe, which is the first thing to understand about it. A plate is assembled to order out of a short list of parts, and the list below is Nick Tahou Hots' own: every item on it is a box you tick on the order form the restaurant publishes for phone and fax orders.
anatomy.srcNote: Read off Nick Tahou Hots' own printable order form on 20 August 2026, plus Visit Rochester's description of what a traditional plate is.

layers.name: Two sides, on the bottom
layers.what: Macaroni salad, home fries, french fries or baked beans. Those four are the whole list on Nick Tahou Hots' order form and you tick the ones you want. Two is the number, and two Rochester kitchens say so in writing: Steve T. Hots & Potatoes prints "Choice of 2 with plates", and Bill Gray's describes its plates as served over 2 side orders. Macaroni salad and home fries is the pair most people mean when they say a plate.

layers.name: The meat, on top of the sides
layers.what: Cheeseburger, hamburger, red hot dog, white hot dog, italian sausage, chicken tender, fried ham, fish fry, grilled cheese, or the veggie plate. Ten choices on the order form, and the red and white hots are a Rochester distinction rather than a typo: a white hot is a pale pork, beef and veal dog that is a local thing in its own right.

layers.name: Hot sauce, poured over the lot
layers.what: The order form calls it Nick's Hot Sauce and it is the thing that makes the plate a plate rather than a tray of sides. It is a loose spiced ground meat sauce, and it goes over the whole plate rather than on one part of it. Fairport Hots is famous, in its own words, for its "Homemade Meat Hot Sauce", which tells you where the argument is around here.

layers.name: Chopped raw onions
layers.what: A tick box on Nick Tahou Hots' order form, and standard unless you say otherwise. Steve T. Hots & Potatoes puts it beyond doubt on its own menu: "On plates, everything includes: Hot Sauce, Mustard, Onions".

layers.name: Mustard
layers.what: The other tick box, and the other third of that same Steve T. line. Yellow mustard, striped over the top.

layers.name: Bread and butter, on the side
layers.what: Italian bread, buttered. Steve T. Hots & Potatoes says its plates are "Served with Italian Bread or Rolls", and Visit Rochester says a plate is usually served with a side of buttered bread. Alex Tahou's account of the original hots and potatoes has two pieces of Italian bread and butter on it as well, so this is the part of the dish that never changed.

listNote: This is a list and not a ranking. Nick Tahou Hots is first because it is where the dish comes from and it holds the trademark, which is a matter of record rather than an opinion about dinner; everything after it is in alphabetical order. Nobody here paid to be on it and there are no affiliate links on this site.
listRule: A place goes on this list only if its OWN site or its OWN online menu says it serves a plate. Being called great on a food blog is not evidence that a kitchen still makes one, and a listing site saying so is worth even less.

places.name: Nick Tahou Hots
places.blurb: Where it comes from and the only kitchen on earth entitled to those two words. It is in the old Buffalo, Rochester & Pittsburgh railroad terminal, a block from Frontier Field, and it has been on this street since 1918.
places.hoursUnknown: Their own site publishes none, and it has not been updated since 2021.
places.note: The second location on West Henrietta Road is gone. Their own site lists West Main and nothing else.

places.name: Bill Gray's
places.blurb: The local chain, and the one you can get to from anywhere in the county. Their own gluten free menu describes a Great Plate as a cheeseburger or hot dog served over 2 side orders, which is the plate build in nine words.
places.hoursUnknown: Their locations page lists thirteen addresses and no hours for any of them.
places.note: No single address here on purpose: it is thirteen shops and picking one would send you past two others.

places.name: Chili Hots
places.blurb: The most complete priced plate menu anybody in this city publishes: thirteen of them, from a $10 Jr Plate up to an $18.50 Shaved Steak Plate, counting a meatless plate, a half plate and a split plate for anyone who has been sensibly warned.
places.hours: Mon to Sat 11am to 10pm, Sun noon to 10pm

places.name: dogTown Hots
places.plateName: Dog Plate, Cheeseburger Plate, Split Plate
places.blurb: The Monroe Avenue hot dog shop, and the one with a vegetarian and vegan plate that people order on purpose rather than as a compromise. Their own site claims a Best Rochester Plate run of more than ten years.
places.hoursUnknown: Their own site reads "Open 11AM to 10:45pm Daily Closed Sundays", which cannot be both, so this page will not pick one for you.
places.note: Their own menu files the dish under two headings that both say Junkyard: Junkyard Plates and Junkyard Dog Plates. The individual plates on those lists are named for the meat, and they publish no prices.

places.name: Empire Hots
places.blurb: Calls itself Home of the Trash Plate on its own front page, and backs it with eleven of them on the menu. This is the clearest example anywhere of what the trademark actually does to a menu: same dish, different two words.
places.hours: Sun to Thu 11am to 10pm, Fri and Sat 11am to midnight

places.name: Fairport Hots
places.plateName: Godfather Plate, Varsity Plate, Jr. Varsity
places.blurb: East side, open late, and the only place on this list that sizes its plates like a football roster. The Godfather is four hots or burgers. Their own words are famous for our Hot Plates, Fish Fry's, and Homemade Meat Hot Sauce.
places.hours: Sun to Wed 10:30am to 11:30pm, Thu 10:30am to midnight, Fri and Sat 10:30am to 1am

places.name: Henrietta Hots
places.blurb: The one nearest RIT, which is most of the explanation. Zweigle's hots, a Friday fish fry, and a plate their own site names but does not price.
places.hours: Mon and Tue 11am to 11pm, Wed to Sat 11am to midnight, Sun 11am to 10pm

places.name: Jeremiah's Tavern
places.area: Monroe Avenue, plus Henrietta, Greece and Penfield
places.blurb: A tavern rather than a hots counter, so this is the version you can sit down and have a beer with. The plate is named after the address: two cheeseburgers, macaroni salad and french fries under burger hot sauce, mustard and onions.
places.hours: Sun to Wed 11am to 11pm, Thu to Sat 11am to midnight
places.note: Three more at 1175 Jefferson Road, 300 Paddy Creek Circle and 2164 Fairport Nine Mile Road, all with their own hours on the locations page. The hours above are Monroe Avenue's.

places.name: The Red Fern
places.blurb: A hundred percent vegan restaurant whose own site calls the Compost Plate their healthy version of Rochester's infamous Garbage Plate. It is the best named plate in the city, and the only one on this list where the whole kitchen is vegan rather than one line of the menu.
places.hours: Tue to Thu 11am to 9pm, Fri and Sat 11am to 9:30pm, closed Sun and Mon
places.note: Last seating is fifteen minutes before close, which their own contact page says and which is easy to lose an evening to.

places.name: Rohrbach Brewing Company
places.blurb: A brewery that put a plate on the menu, which around here counts as civic duty. There is a Bourbon Fried Chicken Plate at $17 and a Das German Plate at $22 beside it.
places.hours: Mon 11am to 9pm, Tue to Thu 11am to 11pm, Fri 11am to midnight, Sat 11:30am to midnight, Sun noon to 9pm
places.note: The Buffalo Road brewpub only. Their Railroad Street beer hall is a different menu with no plate on it, and the kitchen closes an hour before the bar does.

places.name: Steve T. Hots & Potatoes
places.plateName: Hots and Potatoes, and twelve more
places.blurb: The other Tahou counter, and the one still selling the dish under its original name: Hots and Potatoes, $15.00. Open until 3:30am on a Friday, which is the hour this whole dish was invented for.
places.hours: Sun to Thu 10am to midnight, Fri and Sat 10am to 3:30am
places.note: Their own site says the dining room stops seating at 1am every night, so past that it is a counter and a car.

checkedAndLeftOut: Schaller's. Their own menu was read in full on 20 August 2026 and the word plate does not appear on it once: the headings are burgers and sandwiches, extras, drinks and souvenirs. Blogs and directories say they serve a plate. Their menu does not, and a listicle is not evidence a kitchen still makes something.

Mark's Texas Hots. markstexashots.com does not resolve at all, so there is no business-owned source for an address, an hour or a menu. Every listing for it is a directory repeating another directory. Somebody should call them.

Sticky Lips BBQ. Their own site has been reduced to a placeholder reading that it will be available soon, and the page that used to hold the Sticky Icky Plate redirects to it. That is exactly the shape of a closure and this page will not send anybody there on a guess.

Tom Wahl's. Their homepage names no plate, and their menu is served from an ordering platform that returned nothing readable. The Junker plate is widely reported by other people and by nobody at Tom Wahl's.
John's Tex Mex. Their menu page answered 403, so nothing about it could be confirmed from the business.
Hot Shots on Chili Avenue. There is no such restaurant. The Chili Avenue plate shop is Chili Hots and it is on the list above.

photos.file: File:The Garbage Plate, Nick Tahou Hots 2025.jpg
photos.author: Paul Lowry
photos.alt: A Garbage Plate at Nick Tahou Hots: two split white hot dogs lying across home fries and macaroni salad, buried under a layer of crumbled brown meat sauce with chopped raw onion and a line of yellow mustard through it. Two slices of white Italian bread lie on the rim of the plate and a fork rests on the right.
photos.caption: This is the thing itself, photographed at Nick Tahou Hots on 28 June 2025. Two white hots on home fries and macaroni salad, hot sauce poured over the lot, raw onion and mustard on top, bread and butter on the side.

photos.author: Eugene Peretz from Northampton, MA, USA
photos.alt: A Garbage Plate seen from above on a plate whose blue rim reads NICK TAHOU and, along the bottom, HOME OF THE GARBAGE PLATE. Baked beans, macaroni salad and chunky home fries are arranged around the edge; a mound of crumbled meat sauce and chopped onion sits in the middle over a split red hot dog.
photos.caption: Three of the four sides in one frame, photographed in 2007: home fries, macaroni salad and baked beans. The order form lists those three and french fries, and you tick two.

photos.author: Paul Lowry
photos.alt: Two Garbage Plates on a red cafeteria tray, one behind the other. The plate at the back carries split red hot dogs under the meat sauce; the one at the front carries pale white hots. Both sit on the same home fries and macaroni salad. A slice of Italian bread on its own plate and a cup of water stand beside them.
photos.caption: Two plates on one tray, which is the quickest way to see that the meat is a choice and not part of the recipe: red hots at the back, white hots at the front, everything underneath them the same.

photos.author: Eugene Peretz
photos.alt: A large painted sign on the brick wall inside Nick Tahou Hots. It reads NICK TAHOU HOTS in blue over a drawing of a steaming plate of hot dogs, beans and bread, then in script "Home of the Garbage Plate", then Established 1918 in red. A red LED display on the left reads 5 MILLION.
photos.caption: The 1918 date, on the restaurant's own wall in 2007. This page dates the shop and not the dish, and this is one of the two places the business states the shop's date about itself.

photos.author: Doug Kerr
photos.alt: Looking east along West Main Street in Rochester on an overcast day. On the left stands a long red brick building with steep gables and tall arched windows, a hanging sign on it reading NICK TAHOU. A green railroad bridge crosses the road ahead and downtown towers stand behind it.
photos.caption: The building from the street in 2008. The brick block on the left is the old passenger terminal the restaurant moved into, gables and arched windows and all, and the railroad bridge beyond it is the rest of the reason it is there.

photos.file: File:The counter at Nick Tahou Hots' 2025.jpg
photos.author: Paul Lowry
photos.alt: Inside Nick Tahou Hots in 2025. Two customers stand with their backs to the camera at a long blue counter under strip lighting; a member of staff faces them across it. A yellow menu board hangs overhead and a sign on the left wall reads NICK TAHOU HOTS above a drawing of a plate.
photos.caption: The counter, in 2025. Every order here is said out loud across it, which is how a description of somebody else's dinner ended up being the name of the dish.

photos.author: Self
photos.alt: A Garbage Plate held on somebody's lap outdoors on grass. The plate's blue rim reads NICK TAHOU HOTS along the top and, along the bottom, HOME OF THE GARBAGE PLATE. On it are a split red hot dog, home fries, macaroni salad, meat sauce, chopped onion and a heavy pour of ketchup.
photos.caption: The mark, printed around the rim of the plate it belongs to, in May 2005. The photographer released this one into the public domain, so it is the only picture on this page that carries no conditions at all.

photos.author: Paul Lowry
photos.alt: The corner of Nick Tahou Hots' red brick building. A hand-painted board high on the wall carries a Coca-Cola logo and reads NICK TAHOU, PARKING IN REAR OF BUILDING, with a green arrow. Below it a boarded-up window carries a LOTTO sign. A Rochester Heritage Trail marker stands at the curb on the left.
photos.caption: 320 West Main Street, June 2025.

photos.author: DanielPenfield
photos.alt: A Bill Gray's restaurant photographed from its own car park under a clear blue sky. The building is painted dark green and deep red and has two corner towers, each carrying a raised black steam locomotive with a puff of smoke and a curved BILL GRAY'S sign over the top of it. A long BILL GRAY'S sign in deep red letters runs along the right-hand wall beside a blue script Abbott's Frozen Custard sign, and red panels under the awnings read HOME OF THE WORLD'S GREATEST CHEESEBURGER. Young trees and shrubs stand along the front of the building and the marked bays of an empty car park run across the foreground.
photos.caption: Bill Gray's in Henrietta, June 2011, and the only one of the thirteen anybody has photographed under a free license. The photographer's own description on Commons calls it the chain's flagship; their locations page lists thirteen shops and singles out none of them, so that is his word rather than theirs.

photos.author: BanjoZebra
photos.alt: A plate on a mosaic table top: two split red hot dogs lying on chunky home fries and macaroni salad, covered with crumbled brown meat sauce, a scatter of diced raw onion and a zigzag of yellow mustard.
photos.caption: A plate from dogTown, 9 April 2024.
photos.placeNote: The photographer's own description names the restaurant, which is why this is on this card: "Junkyard Plate with hot dogs, macaroni salad, home fries, meat sauce, diced onions, and mustard, from Dogtown in Rochester, New York", and the file's camera position, 43.1439 by -77.5898, is Monroe Avenue at that address. The photographer's title matches the menu: dogTown files the dish under Junkyard Plates, and a second section under Junkyard Dog Plates, read on their own site on 20 August 2026. The individual items under those headings are a Dog Plate, a Cheeseburger Plate, a Split Plate and a Sausage Plate, so the word is the section and not the dish name printed on any one line.

photos.author: BanjoZebra
photos.alt: A Compost Plate on a floral-rimmed china plate: a browned patty under a thick shredded sauce, sitting on a bed of macaroni salad, with a heap of green salad leaves, a slice of bread and a scoop of orange sweet potato around it.
photos.caption: A Compost Plate at The Red Fern, 27 July 2024.
photos.placeNote: The photographer's own description names the restaurant: "Compost Plate at The Red Fern in Rochester, New York", and the file's camera position, 43.1498 by -77.5864, is Oxford Street at that address.

photoNote: Every photograph on this page is somebody else's work under a free license, checked on that file's own page on Wikimedia Commons on 20 August 2026 and re-checked from Commons on every run of scripts/sync-plate-photos.py. Nothing here is hotlinked, cropped or taken from a restaurant, a review site or a search result. The photographer, the license and a link to the license are printed under every picture.
photosRejected: WHAT SEVEN OF THE ELEVEN RESTAURANTS LOOK LIKE. Four of them are on this page in freely licensed photographs and the other seven are not. Bill Gray's joined the three on 20 August 2026, on a second search that went wider than Commons. The other seven were searched a SECOND and then a THIRD time the same day, the third by Wikidata P18, by KartaView and by a re-run of Commons and Openverse against fresh geocodes, and they still have nothing publishable. Those cards carry no picture rather than a borrowed one.

WHERE THE SEARCHES LOOKED, so nobody repeats them. Commons was swept four ways on 20 August 2026: a title search per business, an insource: search of every file description, the local categories (Restaurants in Rochester, Fairport, Henrietta, Chili, Gates, Webster, Monroe County) and a GEOSEARCH of a 1,500m circle around all eight addresses. Commons holds exactly two files naming any of the seven and both are Bill Gray's. Openverse was then swept across roughly forty queries with its license filter set to CC BY, CC BY-SA, CC0 and public domain, which is Flickr and Commons together. Chili Hots, Empire Hots, Fairport Hots, Henrietta Hots, Jeremiah's Tavern and Steve T. Hots return NOTHING under a free license anywhere: what exists of them on Flickr is all NonCommercial or NoDerivatives, and neither is usable here. A THIRD SWEEP THE SAME DAY re-ran all of it against fresh geocodes for the seven addresses and added the queries the first two had not made: insource: on each street NUMBER as well as each name, the category tree under Restaurants in New York (state), and a Commons geosearch at 120m, 600m, 1,500m and 10km around every one of the seven. NOT ONE geotagged Commons file sits within 130m of any of them; the closest is a school 132m from Fairport Hots, and the nearest thing to a restaurant is the takeout-carton photograph already rejected below, 1,255m from Henrietta Hots.

THE FLICKR SWEEPS HAD A HOLE IN THEM AND IT WAS FOUND AND CLOSED ON 20 AUGUST 2026, and it is the reusable half of this whole exercise. Flickr filters a search by numeric license code, and the codes the first two sweeps passed were 4, 5, 7, 8, 9 and 10. That set OMITS 11 and 12, which are CC BY 4.0 and CC BY-SA 4.0, both free and both in active use, so every earlier "nothing free exists" was measured through a filter that could not see two free licenses. All seven names, all seven street names and a 1km geographic search around all seven addresses were re-run with 11 and 12 added. It still comes back empty. The negative holds, and it now holds for the right reason. IF YOU SWEEP FLICKR AGAIN, PASS 4,5,7,8,9,10,11,12.

AND THE SHARPER VERSION OF THE NEGATIVE, which is worth more than "nothing exists" because it says what is actually out there. Photographs of these places DO exist on Flickr and they are not free, read off each result's own license field rather than trusted to a filter: Henrietta Hots was shot by drpep in 2024 and is ALL RIGHTS RESERVED, and Rohrbach has about nine photographs by pearwood, every one of them CC BY-NC-ND. NonCommercial and NoDerivatives both fail here. Three prolific free-license photographers who work this region were identified and cleared one by one: Warren LeMay, who shot Rochester in April 2024 under CC BY-SA 2.0 and photographed downtown landmarks only; Random Retail, who shoots chain retail; and Paul Lowry, whose CC BY 4.0 Rochester food photographs are four of the eleven pictures already on this page and include none of the seven. On Commons the complete upload lists of the region's two most systematic contributors were dumped and searched, 4,529 files by DanielPenfield and 5,000 by Andre Carrotflower, with zero hits. So this is not an absence of searching any more. These are small suburban businesses that nobody has photographed under a free license.

MAPILLARY WAS RE-EXAMINED ON 20 AUGUST 2026 AND HALF OF THE FIRST REJECTION'S REASONING WAS WRONG. This note used to say Mapillary states "no version number anywhere". That was true of mapillary.com/terms and false as a statement about Mapillary. mapillary.com/osm, under the heading "Rights for OpenStreetMap", says in as many words "Mapillary images are available under an open license (CC BY-SA)" and links creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/, and Wikimedia Commons' own Template:Mapillary, which is the template a Commons upload of a Mapillary frame is built from, hardcodes {{cc-by-sa-4.0}} and credits the photographer's USERNAME linked to their Mapillary profile rather than a logo. Both were read on 20 August 2026, the second off the template's own wikitext. So the default license is CC BY-SA 4.0, it carries a version, and a page states it. The sentence that claimed otherwise was a report on ONE page written as a statement about the source, which is the third time that shape of error has been found on this page.

WHAT STILL STOPS MAPILLARY, and both halves were checked this time rather than assumed. Section 3 of the terms grants CC BY-SA "unless we indicate otherwise" and names CC BY-NC-SA as a live alternative, and Mapillary's own API documentation lists every field an Image carries (creator, captured_at, geometry, camera_type, the thumb urls and so on) and there is NO license field among them. So the carve-out has nothing per-image to check it against, and that is a gap in what the API publishes rather than a gap in anybody's search. Section 11 then says that an image "downloaded and served from your own servers" must be attributed "by visibly displaying the Mapillary logo and linking back to the Mapillary homepage or corresponding Mapillary image page", which is a condition on top of naming the photographer rather than instead of it. Read on mapillary.com/terms and the developer documentation on 20 August 2026.

AND THE PRACTICAL BLOCKER, WHICH IS THE ONE TO FIX FIRST AND IS NOT A LICENSE QUESTION AT ALL. Nothing on Mapillary can be reached from this repo without an API token and this repo holds none: every mapillary.com address answers a generic Meta error page, graph.mapillary.com answers "Invalid OAuth 2.0 Access Token", and tiles.mapillary.com answers 403. That means no frame, no photographer's username and no image page, so there is nothing to fetch and nothing to print a credit from. The coverage this note used to quote (70 frames past Bill Gray's, 50 past Fairport Hots, six each past Chili Hots and Empire Hots) could NOT be re-measured on 20 August 2026 and should not be quoted as current. A token is free to register at mapillary.com/developer; put one in .env and this becomes a real lead again rather than an argument.

KARTAVIEW WAS CHECKED THE SAME DAY BECAUSE MAPILLARY COULD NOT BE, and it is the other open street-level library. Its nearby-photos API needs no token, and it does hold Rochester: 101 frames within 300m of downtown. Around the seven it holds nothing that shows a building. The nearest frame to any of them is 312m from Chili Hots and 415m from Jeremiah's Tavern, and Empire Hots, Fairport Hots, Henrietta Hots, Rohrbach and Steve T. Hots have no frame within 600m at all. A frame 300m up the road is a picture of somebody else's building.

WIKIDATA P18 WAS THE ROUTE NOBODY HAD RUN, AND IT WAS RUN ON 20 AUGUST 2026. Only three of the eleven restaurants have a Wikidata item at all, which are Nick Tahou Hots, Bill Gray's and Rohrbach Brewing Company, and a geographic query for businesses within 25km of Rochester returns 19 items and none of the other eight. Rohrbach's item carries a P18 nobody here had seen: File:RohrbachBeer1.JPG, PUBLIC DOMAIN, User:Brian Stiehler, shot 17 September 2010, 3000x4000, a red brick block with Rohrbach's own hanging ROHRBACH THE BREWERY banner on it. The license is perfect and it is the WRONG BUILDING, which was settled off the PHOTOGRAPH rather than off its caption: hanging beside the banner is a second sign reading DEEP DISCOUNT STORAGE, 127 RAILROAD ST. This page's Rohrbach card is the Buffalo Road brewpub, 14.5km from Railroad Street. That is now the second Railroad Street photograph rejected here for the same reason. The same uploader's File:RohrbachBeer2.JPG is brewing tanks indoors in 2008 and names no address at all.

"55/365 Rohrbach Brewing Company", CC BY-SA 2.0, RLHyde (Ryan Hyde), 5 July 2014, verified on its own Flickr page. The license is fine and the file was fetched and looked at. It is an interior door, not a storefront, and what is written across the glass is the TASTING ROOM HOURS: Wed to Fri 10am to 5pm, Saturday 9am to 4pm, tours every hour. Those are twelve years stale, this page's one hard rule is that hours come from the business and nothing else, and a card showing a reader an hours board is a card that gets read instead of the line beside it. It also cannot be placed: the card is the Buffalo Road brewpub only, and nothing in the photograph or its description says which of the two Rohrbach sites it is. Left out on the picture rather than on the license.

"Rohrbach's on Railroad Street", CC BY 2.0, bert_m_b. Free and usable, and it is the WRONG BUILDING: this page's Rohrbach card is the Buffalo Road brewpub, and its own note says the Railroad Street beer hall is a different menu with no plate on it. A correctly licensed photograph of the wrong address is still the wrong address.

File:Rochester Garbage Plate.jpg, CC BY-SA 3.0, Douglas.flowe, 27 November 2013. The license is fine and the file was fetched and looked at. It is a dim phone photograph of a takeout carton and its own description names no restaurant, only "Variation on garbage plate with salt potatoes and bacon", so there is no card it belongs on and nothing it shows that a brighter picture on this page does not. Left out on the picture rather than on the license.

EVERY IMAGE SEARCH RESULT, EVERY RESTAURANT'S OWN SITE AND SOCIAL FEED, EVERY REVIEW SITE, AND STREET VIEW. None of them state a license a static site can meet, and being flattering to a restaurant is not a license from the person who took the photograph. If you want a picture of a place on this list that has none, the two honest routes are to shoot it yourself or to write to the photographer and get it in writing.

WHAT IS STILL GENUINELY UNCHECKED, said out loud so the next person starts here rather than at the beginning. TWO THINGS. Mapillary, which needs an API token this repo does not have, for the reasons three entries above. And PICRYL, which answered 403 from behind Cloudflare on 20 August 2026 to every attempt; it aggregates the Library of Congress, NARA, the Smithsonian and the NYPL, all of which are historical public-domain collections, so a 1990s suburban hot dog stand is unlikely to be in it, but unlikely is not checked. Everything else named on this page is a verified negative.
